text: Deep dives is built: 6 steps,
42 calls the plan did not cover,
and 2 deviations.
It is also the first video whose beats open real pages,
one of each kind.
Step 1 landed.
A beat can carry a detail,
and the player shows an Open chip on it.
Opening pauses the video and shows the page in a side panel;
closing plays on from where you were.
The Open key is O.
While a question is up, O keeps meaning answer in my own words,
rather than opening the chip: a question owns its letters.
That is a deviation, said plainly:
step 1 says E.
But E is Export today, and moving it would break a key reviewers and
a test already rely on.
The panel sits beside the stage rather than over it,
and covers the window only when the stage would drop under 640 pixels.
In the review page, it now sits beside at every window I measured.
Closing plays again only if the video was playing and you have not moved
it, rather than always playing on.
A video that starts by itself surprises you.
Next, part 2: the keys while a page is open,
and step two's pages.
Part 2 of 6.
The chip and the panel are reported.
Now the keys, then the pages.
With a page open, the video's keys are off,
rather than reaching the hidden video;
O and Escape close it.
Open it to press the keys yourself,
with a page or a question up.
Step 2: 7 page templates, from explore to a blank fresh page,
each one self-contained and themed.
One command copies a template into a video,
and the style guide carries the rule:
a detail holds only what the video cannot.
Fresh, the seventh template, is the theme and the bridge around an empty page,
rather than a bridge written from scratch each time,
which is how it breaks.
Data pages are filled from one JSON block,
a prototype from 2 slots, rather than HTML slots everywhere.
Open it to read the block and the slots,
with the lines that carry the call marked.
Each template ships with a worked sample from the uploads plan,
marked sample content, rather than lorem ipsum:
a copied template already shows what good looks like.
Quick check.
Which of these earns a detail:
a page that says 16 megabytes,
the staging runs behind that number,
or the step's title, larger?
Next, part 3: comments inside a page.
Part 3 of 6.
The pages are reported.
Now, commenting on one line of a page.
Step 3: click a row in a page,
and a comment box opens on it,
naming that row.
The comment reaches resolve plan under its step,
with where it points.
Open it to step through one comment's path and see what each part carries.
A comment in a page is an ordinary note plus where it points,
rather than a new kind.
Enter or Escape keep the words;
only the cross throws them away.
A click on a button inside a row works the button,
rather than opening a comment: sorting a table should not start a note.
Plan text shows a link as its words and the address in grey,
rather than a working link: a link is a network load,
and the panel cannot follow it.
Quick check.
You typed a comment on a row,
then press Escape.
Are the words thrown away, saved to the record,
or kept until you close the page?
Next, part 4: what a call opens,
and the plan beside the video.
Part 4 of 6.
Comments are reported.
Now, steps 4 and 5.
Step 4: a call's beat can open a detail,
with Accept and Flag in the panel.
Here, 4 calls open one: a try,
a table, the evidence, and code only where the call is about data.
Accept and Flag in the panel work once,
like the sheet's, and answer the sheet if it is waiting,
rather than letting a verdict change later.
Step 5: the plan's own text sits with the video,
a section per step, the current one ruled in coral;
click one to jump there.
Open it for step 5 as written,
each sentence beside what was built.
The plan text sits beside the stage when that costs under a tenth of
its width, and in the record otherwise.
In the review page it now fits beside at every size;
the widths I measured are one click away.
That is a deviation, said plainly:
step 5 says below the player.
But the record sheet rests over whatever sits below the player,
so no one would find it there.
Next, part 5: step five's last call,
then step 6 and its check.
Part 5 of 6.
The plan beside the video is reported.
Now, one more call on it,
then the check that opens every page.
The plan beside the video is read from plan dot M D,
rather than the resolved plan, which appends review sections the page should not carry.
Step 6: check details runs in finish project and in verify.
A missing page, a network load,
or a page without the bridge stops the build.
This video's 7 pages were each opened in Chromium,
light and dark.
The check fails on 8 more ways a page breaks than the plan named,
like a bridge that never answers a click.
Every rule, fail or warn, with its reason,
is one click away.
Without a browser, the static checks still run and the result says the pages
were not opened, rather than failing the build:
under npx, the browser is not installed.
Next, the last part: the code check,
the 42 calls, and what ran.
Part 6 of 6.
Every step is reported.
Last: what the code check found,
and what 42 calls says about the plan.
Then a fresh agent checked the code.
It caught that this plan's own video has no details,
so this one carries them; and a real bug:
a comment in a page opened from the plan text pointed at the wrong
frame.
Now fixed.
The finding, the fix and the new test are one click away.
42 calls is far too many.
Past about a dozen, the build rules say the plan left too much open,
and it did: it never said how a page is filled,
what the check refuses, or where the plan text goes.
What ran: npm test passes, with the details checks in it.
The code check ran, and every finding is answered.
And check details opened this video's 7 pages.
Not tested: no reviewer has opened a detail in a real review yet;
this video is the first.
Building it found one bug: the review page was too narrow for the panel
or the plan to sit beside the video,
fixed before it shipped.
That is what landed: 6 steps,
15 calls and 2 deviations to judge.
Flag any call, draw on a step to ask for a change,
or accept it.
